lessons.title: Observe
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 2–4 · Activity Book pp. 1–2
lessons.objective: Record three relevant observations and name the sense used for each.
lessons.materials: A fabric swatch, a wooden block, a closed shaker, pencils and a three-row observation table.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils recorded three valid pairs. Follow up with a guided property-and-sense match.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a swatch and a block. Ask which properties pupils can identify using sight or touch.
Describe one visible property and one property they can feel.
Main activity · 30 min
Model one observation using “I notice … using …”. Guide pairs through three stations for sight, touch and hearing.
At each station, observe one item, record its property and name the sense used. Compare entries with a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Check three entries per pupil for a property and a matching sense. Give prompts where an entry is a guess.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 1–2 if available. Independently submit three property-and-sense pairs.
Closure · 5 min
Ask pupils to give one observation that another person could check.
Share a property and name how they checked it.

lessons.title: Classify
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 5–7 · Activity Book pp. 3–4
lessons.objective: Sort six pictures into two groups using one observable feature and state the rule used.
lessons.materials: Animal picture cards and two sorting mats per pair. Use clear full-body pictures.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils sorted all six cards and stated a consistent rule. Revisit one observable feature with pupils who changed rules halfway.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a duck and a goat. Ask pupils to identify a feature visible in one picture only.
Point to a feature and describe the difference.
Main activity · 30 min
Model how one feature produces two groups. Give pairs six cards and ask them to check each card against their rule.
Sort the cards, label each group and explain one decision to a partner. Test a second feature if time permits.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give pictures of a chicken, an owl, a parrot, a cat, a horse and a rabbit. Check that the labels express opposite outcomes of one visible feature and all six placements follow the rule.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 3–4 if available. Individually sort the new pictures, then write or say the rule.
Closure · 5 min
Move one card to the wrong group and ask for a correction.
Move the card back and justify the placement using the feature.

lessons.title: Measure and Use Numbers
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 8–10 · Activity Book pp. 5–6
lessons.objective: Measure two straight paper strips to the nearest centimetre and record both readings with the correct unit.
lessons.materials: 30 cm rulers, pre-cut strips in whole-centimetre lengths and a two-row recording table.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils recorded both measurements with the correct unit. Reteach zero alignment using a marked start line where needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two strips with different starting positions. Ask how to compare their lengths fairly.
Suggest lining up the ends and using the same ruler.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate aligning an end to the zero mark and reading the other end from above. Deliberately start at the 1 cm mark and ask pupils to identify the error.
Take turns measuring and checking with a partner. Record each length in a table with the unit cm.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil two unmarked strips of 8 cm and 14 cm. Check ruler placement and both readings.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 5–6 if available. Independently measure the two strips and label both readings with cm.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what information is missing if a measurement is written as “12”.
Give the unit and explain where to place the strip to start.

lessons.title: Communicate
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 10–11 · Activity Book pp. 7–8
lessons.objective: Present two accurate findings from a tally using a labelled table and one spoken or written comparison.
lessons.materials: Bags of coloured counters, tally sheets and pencils.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils reported two accurate totals and a correct comparison. Revisit the use of headings and reading across a row.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show an unlabelled tally. Ask what a reader needs to know to interpret it.
Suggest labels for what was counted and the number counted.
Main activity · 30 min
Give groups counters in three colours. Model the first table row and ask how the row helps a listener understand the findings.
Count the counters, agree on totals and take turns explaining a finding using their table.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil a new tally showing four red, six blue and two yellow counters. Check the headings, the red and blue totals, and the comparison.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 7–8 if available. Convert the tally into a labelled table independently, then report the red and blue totals and say which colour has more.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what would make a classmate's table easy to understand.
Identify one useful feature, such as clear category headings.

lessons.title: Use Apparatus and Handle Specimens
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 12–14 · Activity Book pp. 9–10 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Independently use a dropper to wet cotton wool without pooling water and place two seeds gently with blunt tweezers.
lessons.materials: Water, plastic droppers, shallow clear cups, cotton wool, dried beans, blunt tweezers and trays. Tell pupils the beans are for observation.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils met all three checks. Give pupils who squeezed too much water a short dropper practice task.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two prepared cups, one with damp cotton wool and one with pooled water. Ask which tool helps control the amount.
Choose a dropper and describe the difference between the cups.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate drawing water into the dropper and adding it a few drops at a time. Show how to lift a bean gently over the tray.
Take turns preparing a cup. Stop when the cotton wool is evenly damp and place two beans apart so both can be seen.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil a clean setup and check dropper use, absence of pooled water, and careful transfer of both seeds.
Independently prepare one cup, then explain how the dropper or tweezers helped. Refer to the relevant items in Activity Book pp. 9–10 if available.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how to correct a setup with too much water.
Explain how adding a few drops at a time prevents pooling.

lessons.title: Sketch and Clean Apparatus
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 12–14 · Activity Book pp. 9–10 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Make a recognisable sketch with three correct labels and clean the plastic cup and dropper without leaving visible residue.
lessons.materials: A clear plastic cup with a bean and damp cotton wool, plastic dropper, shallow tray, clean rinse water and a draining rack. Prepare a second cup and dropper used with water and a pinch of sugar for cleaning practice.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils completed the sketch and cleaning checks. Reteach the sketch or rinsing step that each pupil missed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a simple line drawing of a cup and ask what would make the specimen inside easy to identify.
Suggest showing the bean outline and adding a clear label.
Main activity · 30 min
Model drawing from the side, then show how to rinse a used cup and draw and expel clean water through the dropper over the tray.
Practise sketching the cup setup with a partner. Take turns rinsing the used cup and dropper and placing them on the rack.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Check each pupil's sketch for a clear outline and correct labels for the cup, bean and cotton wool. Observe each pupil rinsing both items and checking for residue.
Sketch and label the setup independently. Clean the used cup and dropper, then show both items to the teacher.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why a dropper used for sugar solution still needs rinsing if the liquid looks clear.
Explain that clear liquid can still contain dissolved sugar, then describe how to rinse the dropper.

lessons.title: Store Apparatus and Substances
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 12–14 · Activity Book pp. 9–10 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Return three items to their designated places and explain what to do with a wet cup before storage.
lessons.materials: A clean dry plastic cup, a clean dry plastic dropper, a closed labelled container of table sugar, a wet cup, an equipment tray, a substance shelf and a drying rack.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils stored all three items correctly and identified the drying step. Repeat the routine with pupils who mixed equipment and substances.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a wet cup beside a dry cup. Ask which is ready to put away.
Choose the dry cup and give one reason.
Main activity · 30 min
Model checking that apparatus is clean and dry and that the substance lid is closed. Point out the storage labels and drying rack.
In pairs, check sample items, choose the correct location and explain why a wet item goes to the rack.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Observe each pupil returning a dry cup, a dry dropper and the closed sugar container. Check all three locations and the response to the wet cup.
Put the three items away independently. Point to the drying rack and explain when the wet cup can be stored.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what to check before returning the sugar container.
Check the label and confirm that the lid is closed.

lessons.title: Follow Science Room Rules
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 18–20 · Activity Book pp. 11–12
lessons.objective: Follow the agreed entry, incident-reporting and clean-up routines during a practical activity, and explain how one rule prevents harm.
lessons.materials: Plastic cups, plastic spoons, water, trays, cleaning cloths, incident picture cards and a pupil checklist. Use a picture to simulate a spill or damaged item.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils followed all three routines independently and explained one safety reason. Practise the missed routine with pupils who needed a prompt before the next practical activity.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Mark the bag area and show how to keep the walkway clear. Record each pupil's entry action on the checklist.
Leave bags in the agreed area, walk to the assigned station and wait for instructions.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate transferring a spoonful of water between cups over a tray. Show an incident card to one group at a time and observe how each pupil reports it.
Take turns moving water over the tray. When shown an incident card, stop, leave the affected item alone and tell the teacher where it is and what happened.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Observe each pupil clean and return one item. Use three checklist columns for entry, reporting and clean-up. Recheck an action after a short prompt where needed.
Clean and return assigned equipment independently. Explain to the teacher or write how a clear walkway or immediate reporting keeps people safe.
Closure · 5 min
Review the response to a damaged item and ask which action to take first.
State the first action. Use Activity Book pp. 11–12 for follow-up if available.

lessons.title: Human Reproduction
lessons.references: Textbook p. 24 · Activity Book p. 13
lessons.objective: State that humans reproduce by giving birth and select the picture that shows a new human entering a family.
lessons.materials: Teacher-made cards showing a newborn with a caregiver, an older child, and an unrelated picture of an egg hatching.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils selected the correct picture and stated how humans reproduce. Revisit the vocabulary using the newborn card.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a picture of a newborn with a caregiver. Ask which person has just been born.
Point to the newborn and describe what they see.
Main activity · 30 min
Introduce the words human, newborn and giving birth. Compare the two human cards and ask which represents the arrival of a new baby.
Sort the pictures, match the newborn card to the phrase “giving birth” and say how humans reproduce.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Show three new drawings: a newborn with a caregiver, a child reading and a chick hatching. Ask “Which drawing shows a human who has just been born?” and “How do humans reproduce?”
Independently select the newborn picture and answer the second question in a sentence.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for the key sentence again and connect it to the next lesson on changes after birth.
State that humans reproduce by giving birth.

lessons.title: Describe Growth Since Birth
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 25–27 · Activity Book pp. 14–15
lessons.objective: Use the records for one fictional child to describe the changes in body size, height and weight between birth and age seven.
lessons.materials: Stage cards and a fictional record showing 50 cm and 3 kg at birth and 120 cm and 23 kg at age seven, with two illustrations of the same child.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils described all three changes and cited one pair of readings. Revisit the units with pupils who confused height and weight.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the child's two pictures. Ask how the earlier and later stages differ.
Identify the baby and the older child and name one visible change.
Main activity · 30 min
Model reading a two-row growth record. Ask which column shows height and which shows weight. Use pictures to discuss body size.
Put the stage cards in order and use the record and pictures to make one statement about each change.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give a new fictional example, with 49 cm and 3 kg at birth and 117 cm and 21 kg at age seven. Check all three statements against the pictures and record.
Independently describe the changes in body size, height and weight. Cite one pair of readings as evidence.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how to distinguish what was seen in the picture from what was read in the record.
Identify the evidence used for body size and for one measured change.

lessons.title: Compare Growth Among Individuals
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 28–30 · Activity Book p. 16
lessons.objective: Compare two sets of measurements for fictional children of the same age and use at least two findings to conclude that individuals can grow differently.
lessons.materials: Teacher-made paper hand outlines with pre-checked lengths, rulers and anonymised model records. Do not collect pupils' own body measurements.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils used two accurate findings to support the conclusion. Repeat one comparison using a side-by-side table where needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two different hand outlines labelled “Age 7”. Ask whether equal age means equal size.
Suggest a measurement that could test the idea.
Main activity · 30 min
Model measuring hand length from a marked wrist line to the longest fingertip. Give pairs two outlines and the matching fictional height records.
Measure both outlines, record the lengths and compare them alongside the heights. Discuss why one measurement cannot describe all growth.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give a fresh pair of outlines measuring 12 cm and 14 cm, with heights of 123 cm and 118 cm. Check two accurate comparisons and an evidence-based conclusion.
Independently measure the outlines and write one comparison about hand length, one about height and one conclusion.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what the examples show about children of the same age.
Explain that their measurements can differ and point to one result.

lessons.title: Recognise Inherited Features
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 30–32 · Activity Book pp. 17–20 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Explain that features can be inherited from parents or earlier generations and identify two possible inherited features in a fictional family chart.
lessons.materials: Illustrated fictional family charts and feature cards for iris colour, hair type and skin colour.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils identified two examples and explained inheritance. Revisit feature categories with a labelled picture.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two fictional relatives with the same hair type. Ask pupils to describe the feature.
Describe the shared hair type using the illustration.
Main activity · 30 min
Model reading a fictional family chart across two generations. Explain that a shared feature may be inherited and that a picture alone cannot tell which relative it came from.
Circle two shared features and discuss why clothing or a hairstyle chosen for the day is a different kind of similarity.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give a fictional chart showing that Aina and her mother have brown irises, and Aina and her grandfather have wavy hair. Check both examples and the explanation.
Independently name two possible inherited features, identify the people who share them and explain the idea in one sentence.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for one feature pupils can compare on a chart.
Name a feature and point to an example in the fictional chart.

lessons.title: Communicate Findings About Growth and Heredity
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 33–34 · Activity Book pp. 19–20
lessons.objective: Communicate one growth observation and one possible inherited feature, giving relevant evidence for both from a fictional case.
lessons.materials: Case cards with two dated height readings and a fictional family illustration, pencils and a two-box response sheet.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils gave both findings with supporting evidence. Provide the sentence stem “I know this because …” for the missing explanation.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a height record and a fictional family chart. Ask which source answers a question about change over time.
Choose the height record and explain why it has two readings.
Main activity · 30 min
Model a growth statement supported by two readings and an inheritance statement supported by a shared feature. Offer a labelled sketch or short oral report.
Prepare a two-part explanation with a partner and check that the evidence matches each statement.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give a new case with heights of 104 cm and 121 cm and a chart showing shared curly hair. Check one supported finding of each type.
Independently present both findings through a labelled sketch, two short written statements or an oral explanation.
Closure · 5 min
Ask pupils to name the evidence that makes one of their statements clear.
Point to the two readings or the shared feature in the chart.

lessons.title: How Animals Reproduce
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 36–37 · Activity Book pp. 21–22 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: State the two ways animals reproduce shown in the textbook and give one correct example of each.
lessons.materials: Picture pairs showing a duck with eggs and a goat with its young, plus picture cards of a crocodile nest and an elephant calf.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils stated both ways and gave a correct example for each. Repeat the picture-to-phrase match where needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a duckling and a kid. Ask how each came into the world.
Make a prediction for each animal.
Main activity · 30 min
Reveal the picture evidence and model the phrases “lays eggs” and “gives birth to live young”. Introduce the crocodile and elephant cards and ask which phrase fits each.
Match a phrase to each picture pair and explain their choices to a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Hand out an exit slip showing a duck and an elephant with their young. Ask pupils to state the two ways and label each example.
Independently write or say “lays eggs” and “gives birth to live young”, then match them to the duck and elephant.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for one example of each way and point to the matching pictures.
State the two examples in full sentences.

lessons.title: Classify Animals by Reproduction
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 36–38 · Activity Book pp. 21–22 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Classify at least five of six animals by their way of reproducing and justify one choice using a clue.
lessons.materials: Two-column sorting mat and illustrated clues for duck, crocodile, mosquito, goat, bat and elephant.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils placed at least five animals correctly and justified one choice. Revisit the evidence on any misplaced card.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Hold up a bat and a duck card. Ask what evidence would tell us how each reproduces.
Suggest looking for eggs or evidence of a live birth.
Main activity · 30 min
Model sorting a duck using a picture of its nest. Give teams the clue cards and ask them to read the evidence before they place each animal.
Sort the cards, then swap one example with another team and explain its placement.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil a shuffled six-card sheet with short clues. Check for at least five correct placements and one justification.
Independently place the animals in the two groups and explain one choice using its clue.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why a duck and a bat can both fly and still belong in different groups.
Identify the way each reproduces as the sorting rule.

lessons.title: Animals That Lay Few or Many Eggs
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 39–40 · Activity Book p. 23
lessons.objective: Use two observation pictures to explain one example of an animal that lays few eggs and one that lays many eggs.
lessons.materials: Swan nest and frogspawn illustrations, counters for the swan nest, and an illustrated observation sheet with a swan and a fish example.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils explained both examples with picture evidence. Revisit the few-versus-many comparison with counters.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Display a swan nest and a frogspawn picture side by side. Ask which has more visible eggs.
Point to the picture with more eggs and describe the clue.
Main activity · 30 min
Use counters to represent the eggs in the illustrated swan nest. Show a large cluster of frog eggs and ask pupils to compare the observations.
Make a sketch of each observation and describe which animal laid few eggs and which laid many in the examples.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give pupils a swan-nest illustration and a fish-egg cluster with the animal named. Check one evidence-based sentence for each picture.
Independently name the animals, use “few” or “many” for each and refer to the eggs shown.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for one pair of examples from the lesson.
Compare the swan and frog examples in one sentence.

lessons.title: Animals That Give Birth to Few or Many Young
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 41–42 · Activity Book p. 24
lessons.objective: Give one example each of an animal that gives birth to few and many young, supported by the number shown in an illustrated birth record.
lessons.materials: Model birth records for an elephant with one calf, a rabbit with six kits, a dolphin with one calf and a cat with five kittens.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils gave both examples and supported them with the counts shown. Repeat the comparison using counters if needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show an elephant birth record and ask how many young were born in that record.
Count the calf and state the number.
Main activity · 30 min
Compare the elephant record with the rabbit record. Ask what the two examples show about the number born at a time.
Fill a two-row table with animal, number born and “few” or “many”. Explain the comparison to a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give the dolphin and cat records. Ask pupils to compare them and check the names and evidence.
Independently write or say that the dolphin is the “few” example and the cat is the “many” example, citing the two counts.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what pupils looked at to decide between “few” and “many”.
State that they compared how many young were born in the examples.

lessons.title: Record Changes During Animal Growth
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 45–46 · Activity Book pp. 25–27
lessons.objective: Sequence four illustrated frog life-cycle stages and record two observable changes between stages.
lessons.materials: Frog and cow life-cycle illustrations, four shuffled frog cards and a recording strip.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils ordered four stages and recorded two supported changes. Revisit the pair of stages pupils confused.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a tadpole and an adult frog. Ask pupils to point to one visible difference.
Describe a feature such as the tail or legs.
Main activity · 30 min
Model how to record the appearance of a stage from an illustration. Use calf and adult cow illustrations to practise recording an observation, then distribute the frog cards.
Sequence frog eggs, tadpole, froglet and adult frog. Discuss the froglet’s legs and the shorter tail, then compare the froglet with the adult frog.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Hand out a fresh four-image frog strip in a different order. Check the sequence and two changes between neighbouring stages.
Independently number the stages and record two changes using arrows, labelled sketches or short phrases.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which pair of images supports one change.
Point to two stages and read out the change.

lessons.title: Compare Young Animals and Their Adults
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 43–44 · Activity Book p. 28
lessons.objective: Compare two young-and-adult pairs and support each comparison with a visible feature.
lessons.materials: Paired pictures of a kitten and adult cat, a calf and adult cow, a caterpillar and adult butterfly, and a tadpole and adult frog.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils made two accurate comparisons with visible features. Revisit the comparison using labelled pictures.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the kitten and adult cat. Ask which features can be seen on both.
Identify a shared feature such as four legs.
Main activity · 30 min
Model using the same feature to compare both pictures. Contrast the adult butterfly's wings with the caterpillar picture.
Match young animals to their adults and mark a visible similarity or difference on each pair.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give pupils the cow and frog pairs. Check one comparison supported by a feature for each pair.
Independently explain how the calf resembles the cow and how the tadpole differs from the adult frog.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for one example of a young animal that looks noticeably different from its adult.
Name the example and point to the feature that supports it.

lessons.title: Communicate Observations About Reproduction and Growth
lessons.references: Textbook p. 46 and p. 48 · Teacher-made assessment
lessons.objective: Communicate one observation about reproduction and two about growth using evidence from one illustrated life cycle.
lessons.materials: Butterfly life-cycle pictures showing an adult laying eggs, a caterpillar, a chrysalis and an adult butterfly, plus paper for labelled sketches.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils communicated all three observations with picture evidence. Offer a three-box prompt for the missing observation.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a butterfly laying eggs and ask pupils which detail tells us how it reproduces.
Point to the eggs and describe what the adult does.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate how to mark the reproduction observation separately from changes in growth on a simple picture sequence. Give pairs a set of cycle pictures.
Rehearse a short report with a partner. Point to the egg-laying image and explain two changes shown across the pictures.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Invite each pupil to make a labelled sketch, write a short report or give an oral account. Check the reproduction observation and two growth observations against the pictures.
Independently communicate that the adult lays eggs, that a caterpillar hatches and that an adult with wings emerges from the chrysalis, or give other supported observations.
Closure · 5 min
Invite one pupil to share an observation and show its evidence.
Listen and locate the matching picture.

lessons.title: Explain Why Plants Are Important
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 49–50 · Activity Book p. 29
lessons.objective: Give one example of how a plant helps people and one of how a plant helps an animal, with the benefit named in each example.
lessons.materials: Pictures of rice, a mango tree, a bird nest in a tree and a caterpillar feeding on leaves; two-column recording slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils named both recipients and their benefits correctly. Revisit the picture clues with pupils who named a plant without a benefit.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a rice plant beside a bowl of rice and ask how the pictures are connected.
Describe the link between the plant and the food.
Main activity · 30 min
Model a benefit statement using the rice pictures. Give pairs pictures of the tree, nest and feeding caterpillar and ask what each animal gets from a plant.
Sort the examples into food and shelter, then explain a picture using “The plant provides … for …”.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Show a mango fruit eaten by a person and a bird sheltering in a tree. Check one correct benefit for each recipient.
Independently write or say that the mango tree provides food for a person and that the tree provides shelter for the bird.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what the caterpillar gets from the plant and how pupils can tell.
Name food as the benefit and point to the feeding evidence.

lessons.title: Identify What Seeds Need to Germinate
lessons.references: Textbook p. 51 · Activity Book pp. 30–31
lessons.objective: State the three conditions needed for seed germination and identify the missing condition in two illustrated examples.
lessons.materials: Dry and germinated mung beans; teacher-made condition cards showing moist cotton at room temperature, dry cotton, reduced access to air and a cold location.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils identified both missing conditions and stated all three needs. Review the condition cards with pupils who confuse a seed's needs with those of a growing plant.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Compare a dry seed with a germinated seed. Ask what visible change tells us germination has started.
Point to the root emerging from the seed and describe the change.
Main activity · 30 min
Introduce water, air and a suitable temperature. Show a reference condition and compare one changed condition at a time using the cards.
Match condition cards to water, air or temperature. Predict which condition is suitable and explain why.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil a dry-cotton case and a cold-location case with the other conditions stated. Ask pupils to identify each missing condition and list all three needs.
Independently identify water and a suitable temperature in the respective cases, then state all three germination needs.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what “suitable temperature” means for the seed shown.
Explain that the seed needs a temperature at which it can germinate.

lessons.title: Record Changes From Seed to Seedling
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 52–53 · Activity Book p. 32
lessons.objective: Record the height and number of visible leaves at three observed stages of mung-bean growth and describe two changes using the records.
lessons.materials: Living mung-bean specimens prepared in advance at three stages, labels showing days since sowing, rulers and individual observation tables.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils completed the three records and described two supported changes. Repeat the measurement or counting method where results were inconsistent.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a newly germinated seed and an older seedling. Ask what could be measured or counted.
Suggest comparing the height or counting visible leaves.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate measuring each specimen from its support surface to the shoot tip and agree which visible leaves to count. Guide groups to visit the labelled specimens in order.
Observe the real seeds and seedlings, measure and count using the same method, then compare observations within the group.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil to complete a three-row table and describe two changes supported by their own observations. Check the units and the match between each conclusion and its data.
Record the day, height in centimetres and leaf count, then compare two stages using the recorded values.
Closure · 5 min
Invite a pupil to point to the values that support one observed change.
Read out the values and describe the change.

lessons.title: Sequence the Stages of Plant Growth
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 54–55 · Activity Book pp. 33–34
lessons.objective: Arrange five stages of a flowering plant's growth and explain one visible change between adjacent stages.
lessons.materials: Labelled tomato sequence for modelling, shuffled okra stage cards and a five-box recording strip.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils ordered all five stages and explained a change. Revisit any swapped stages using the visual clue on each card.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a flower and a fruit from the same kind of plant. Ask which appeared first.
Predict the order and give a reason.
Main activity · 30 min
Model using a visible clue to place a germinating seed after a seed. Give groups the tomato cards and ask them to check each pair of neighbouring stages.
Arrange seed, germination, young plant, flowering and fruiting. Point to a clue that distinguishes each neighbouring pair.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil shuffled okra pictures. Check the five positions and one explanation that uses picture evidence.
Independently order and label the pictures, then explain a change such as flowers appearing after the young plant stage.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which picture shows that the seed has started to grow.
Identify the germination picture and point to the emerging root.

lessons.title: Investigate What Plants Need to Grow
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 56–58 · Activity Book p. 35
lessons.objective: Compare two plants in a fair watering investigation and use a recorded observation to explain why water matters, then name air and sunlight as further needs and nutrients as supporting growth.
lessons.materials: Two similar seedlings in identical pots, dated class observations from a seven-day investigation, labels, a measuring cup and a comparison sheet.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils drew the water conclusion from evidence and identified the other requirements. Compare the original records again where pupils give a prediction as an observation.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the two plants and ask which differences pupils can observe.
Describe the leaves or stem of each plant.
Main activity · 30 min

Review the class investigation. Both pots received the same light and growing medium, with watering as the changed condition. Ask pupils to compare the first- and seventh-day records. Use the textbook results to discuss air, sunlight and the role of nutrients.
Compare the live plants and the records, identify what changed and what was kept the same, then point to evidence for the effect of watering.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil to complete one evidence sentence about water and label a plant diagram with its further needs and the role of nutrients.
Independently describe a recorded difference, link it to watering, name air and sunlight, and explain that nutrients help plants grow.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why both pots were kept in the same place.
Explain that the comparison used the same light for both plants.

lessons.title: Explain Observations About a Plant's Life
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 57–59 · Activity Book p. 36
lessons.objective: Explain two observations from a plant record and use them to predict one effect of interrupted growth on a person or an animal.
lessons.materials: Dated class sketches or photos of a seed and seedling, pictures of a healthy and a wilted plant, and a three-box storyboard.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils explained two supported observations and gave a plausible prediction. Use the storyboard to revisit any missing link.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two dated plant observations and ask which changes can be seen.
Identify a visible change between the records.
Main activity · 30 min
Model how to connect an observation to an explanation. Compare conditions for germination with those for later growth and discuss an example of a plant used for food.
In pairs, rehearse a short explanation using two dated records and predict what could happen if plants stop growing before they produce food.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask pupils to explain two observations and one consequence using a labelled sketch, short writing or an oral explanation. Check the distinction between observations and prediction.
Independently explain two visible changes using the records and predict a consequence, such as fewer leaves available for a leaf-eating animal.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which statement came directly from the observation and which described a possible future outcome.
Identify one observation and the prediction based on it.

lessons.title: Recognise Numbers
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 2–5 · Activity Book pp. 1–2
lessons.objective: Say one number shown as a numeral and read one number shown in words, then match at least four of five numerals to their word forms.
lessons.materials: Number and word cards, including pairs such as 306 and 360.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils read both formats and matched at least four pairs. Practise numbers with a zero in tens or ones where needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show 306 and 360. Ask what changes when the zero moves.
Read the two numbers and compare what they hear.
Main activity · 30 min
Model reading a three-digit number in place-value order. Give pairs shuffled numeral and word cards.
Match the cards. Read the written form and say the number on the numeral card to verify each match.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Show 520 and the words “seven hundred and two” as separate oral prompts. Check the five independent matches for 217, 260, 402, 420 and 618.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 1–2 if available. Match the five numbers to shuffled word cards independently and read both oral prompts to the teacher.
Closure · 5 min
Show 614 and 641 and ask which numeral matches “six hundred and fourteen”.
Choose a numeral and say it aloud.

lessons.title: Write Numbers
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 6–7 · Activity Book pp. 3–4
lessons.objective: Write at least four of five numbers correctly, including one conversion in each direction between numerals and words.
lessons.materials: Mini-whiteboards, place-value mats and a five-item response slip.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils scored at least four of five with success in both directions. Reteach the conversion direction that caused errors.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Say “four hundred and seven”. Show 407 and 470 and ask which one matches.
Choose a numeral and explain what the zero represents.
Main activity · 30 min
Use a hundreds-tens-ones mat to model 805, then show how to write it in words. Give pairs alternating numeral and word prompts.
Write each number in the other form and check a partner's response against the mat.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give “two hundred and eight” and “six hundred and thirty” for pupils to write in numerals, and 315, 470 and 906 to write in words. Note recurring zero or digit-order errors.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 3–4 if available. Complete the five conversions independently.
Closure · 5 min
Present one swapped-digit answer and ask pupils to correct it.
Write the correct answer and explain the change.

lessons.title: Show and Match Number Values
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 8–12 · Activity Book pp. 5–6
lessons.objective: Build two numbers using base-ten blocks and correctly match two block pictures to their numerals.
lessons.materials: Base-ten blocks, block pictures and numeral cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils completed all four items. Rebuild a zero-place example with pupils who added blocks to fill an empty column.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a unit cube, a ten rod and a hundred flat. Ask what quantity each represents.
Name each quantity and explain how ten unit cubes form a ten.
Main activity · 30 min
Model 284 with blocks. Provide a mixture of numeral cards and pictures, including numbers with zero tens or ones.
Build a number from a numeral, then switch roles and match a pictured group to its numeral.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask pupils to build 307 and 460. Show pictures of two flats, five rods and one cube, and of six flats and two cubes. Check the two builds and the matches to 251 and 602.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 5–6 if available. Build and match the four items independently.
Closure · 5 min
Show a group with four hundred flats and three unit cubes.
Hold up 403 and explain why no ten rods are needed.

lessons.title: Place Value and Digit Value
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 13–15 · Activity Book pp. 7–9
lessons.objective: State both the place and digit value of a marked digit in at least three of four examples.
lessons.materials: Place-value mats, digit cards and mini-whiteboards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils answered at least three items correctly. Use a place-value mat to distinguish the column name from the amount represented.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show 242. Point to the two 2s and ask what each represents.
Describe the difference between the value of the first and last 2.
Main activity · 30 min
Model “The place is tens. The digit value is 40.” Move a digit across columns and ask pupils to describe its new value.
Use a mat to change the digit positions, then give the place and digit value for a partner's marked digit.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Mark 3 in 318, 2 in 425, 9 in 619 and 0 in 708. Count an item correct when both the place and digit value are correct.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 7–9 if available. Write both answers for each marked digit independently.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for the place and digit value of 0 in 503.
State “tens” and “zero” and point to the tens column.

lessons.title: Partition Numbers
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 16–17 · Activity Book pp. 10–11
lessons.objective: Partition two of three numbers correctly in both forms, using place names and expanded sums.
lessons.materials: Digit cards, place-value mats and response slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils wrote both forms for at least two numbers. Provide a place-value mat to pupils who used a digit in place of its value.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Display 300 + 50 + 8 and ask pupils to combine the parts.
Build 358 and name the three groups.
Main activity · 30 min
Model 705 as seven hundreds, zero tens and five ones, then as 700 + 5. Use the mat to show why both forms represent the same number.
Partition three-digit numbers in both forms. Check each answer by recombining its parts.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 436, 802 and 570. Check that the values add to the original number and that the two forms agree.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 10–11 if available. Write both partitions for each number independently.
Closure · 5 min
Show 650 as 600 + 5 and ask pupils to repair the error.
Write 600 + 50 and explain the value of 5 in the tens place.

lessons.title: Compare Numbers
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 18–21 · Activity Book pp. 12–13
lessons.objective: Correctly compare at least three of four pairs of numbers up to 1,000 and explain one comparison using place value.
lessons.materials: Numeral cards, hundreds-tens-ones mats and a number line.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils compared at least three pairs and explained one. Revisit highest-place comparisons with pupils who relied on the ones digit.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show 391 and 319. Ask which number is greater and which column settles it.
Compare from the hundreds column and explain why the tens decide.
Main activity · 30 min
Model comparing from the highest place. Include pairs with equal hundreds and equal tens. Extend the mat to thousands when comparing with 1,000 and check one comparison on a number line.
Arrange cards from each pair, tell a partner which number is greater and name the first place that differs.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give pairs 327 and 372, 608 and 604, 95 and 205, and 999 and 1,000. Check four comparisons and ask pupils to justify one using the deciding place.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 12–13 if available. Independently write four “greater than” or “less than” comparisons and explain one.
Closure · 5 min
Present 599 and 600 and ask what decides the comparison.
Choose 600 and explain that six hundreds exceed five hundreds.

lessons.title: Arrange Numbers
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 22–23 · Activity Book pp. 14–15
lessons.objective: Arrange four pictured quantities correctly from least to greatest and from greatest to least.
lessons.materials: Cards showing groups of hundred flats, ten rods and unit cubes, with separate numeral labels.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils ordered all four collections in both directions. Revisit the first differing place when two values were swapped.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show three pictured collections and ask which has the smallest quantity.
Compare the groups and point to the smallest.
Main activity · 30 min
Model how to label the collections, find the smallest and compare the two closest values. Reverse the row and name both directions.
Match numerals to pictured collections, then build two rows in opposite orders and read each row aloud.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give four pictured quantities: 209, 290, 219 and 201. Check both full rows and ask which two are closest to 209 in the ascending row.
Arrange the picture cards independently in both orders and record the two numeral sequences.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what happens to the smallest group when the row is reversed.
Identify the new position and state whether the row increases or decreases.

lessons.title: Count Numbers and Complete Sequences
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 24–28 · Activity Book pp. 16–18
lessons.objective: Count forward in tens and backward in hundreds for three steps each, and fill at least three of four missing terms in given sequences.
lessons.materials: Number lines, ten rods, hundred flats and sequence slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils counted both runs and filled at least three blanks. Practise counting across a hundred boundary as needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Start at 190 and ask what comes next when one ten is added.
Show one ten rod and say 200.
Main activity · 30 min
Model stepping forward in tens from 470 and back in hundreds from 920. Show how an empty position represents a whole step.
Move counters or mark jumps on a number line, say each landing number and explain one missing term to a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Listen to three steps from 280 in tens and three from 840 back in hundreds. Check blanks in 197, __, 199, __ and 960, __, 760, __.
Count both short runs and fill the four blanks independently.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how to check a missing term when a number on either side is given.
Show a jump from one side and check it against the other.

lessons.title: Estimate Numbers
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 29–31 · Activity Book pp. 19–20
lessons.objective: Give a reasonable estimate for two groups of objects and justify each estimate using a known reference quantity.
lessons.materials: Equal-size grid cards, a reference card with 20 dots, and target cards with 37 and 62 dots arranged at similar spacing.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils gave two plausible estimates with a reference-based reason. Offer a matching grid overlay to pupils who guessed without comparing.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Display a card with 20 dots and a card with a larger group. Ask for an estimate using the known group.
Compare the areas covered and suggest how many groups of 20 might fit.
Main activity · 30 min
Model using one section of a grid as a reference and combining approximate groups. Count one practice card afterwards to check the estimate.
Estimate in pairs using a phrase such as “about two groups of 20”. Count afterwards and discuss how close the estimate was.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Show the 37-dot and 62-dot cards. Accept 30–50 and 50–70 respectively for these cards when pupils explain each estimate using the 20-dot reference.
Independently give an estimate for each card and explain it in terms of the reference group before counting to check.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how a known group helps when there are too many objects to count quickly.
Explain how to compare the unknown group with the reference.

lessons.title: Round to the Nearest Hundred
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 34–35 · Activity Book pp. 22–23 (shared rounding reference)
lessons.objective: Round at least three of four whole numbers correctly to the nearest hundred and explain one decision using the midpoint.
lessons.materials: Open number lines, hundreds cards and mini-whiteboards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils rounded at least three correctly and explained one. Revisit the midpoint with pupils who rounded 350 down.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Place 417 between 400 and 500. Ask which hundred is closer.
Point to the nearer hundred and describe the distance.
Main activity · 30 min
Model locating 249, 250 and 251 between 200 and 300. Mark the midpoint and model the convention of rounding halfway up.
Place each number on the line and explain whether it lies below, on or above the midpoint.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 349, 350, 680 and 951. Check at least three correct rounded values and one midpoint explanation.
Independently round all four numbers to the nearest hundred and show a number line for one.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how 951 can round to 1,000.
Identify 900 and 1,000 as the endpoints and explain that 951 is past 950.

lessons.title: Identify and Complete Number Patterns
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 36–39 · Activity Book pp. 24–26
lessons.objective: State the direction and step size of two patterns and fill at least three of four missing terms.
lessons.materials: Number cards, dry-erase sleeves and arrows labelled with step sizes.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils stated both rules and filled at least three blanks. Use labelled arrows to revisit direction or step size.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show 355, 360, 365 and ask what changes between consecutive terms.
Say that each number increases by five.
Main activity · 30 min
Model checking the same difference between more than one pair of terms. Show a decreasing pattern and one where a gap covers two steps.
Mark the step on arrows, explain the rule to a partner and fill missing positions on a card strip.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 246, 256, __, 276, __ and 740, 640, __, 440, __. Check both rules and the four missing terms.
Independently write the two rules and fill all four blanks.
Closure · 5 min
Show 425, 435, 445, 465 and ask which entry breaks the pattern.
Replace 465 with 455 and justify the correction using the step size.

lessons.title: Solve Everyday Number Problems
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 40–43 · Activity Book pp. 27–28
lessons.objective: Solve two everyday whole-number problems and show a suitable representation and a sentence answering each question.
lessons.materials: Task cards, place-value charts and blank number lines.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils solved both problems and showed their reasoning. Give a short representation-matching task to pupils who used the wrong clues.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a locker clue with a 5 in hundreds and 0 in tens. Ask what extra information would identify its number.
Identify the missing ones digit.
Main activity · 30 min
Model underlining useful facts in a short problem. Demonstrate a place-value chart for a digit clue and a number line for finding a missing value between two known values.
Choose a representation for each practice problem, solve it in pairs and explain how the solution fits the clues.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give two tasks: a delivery code with 6 hundreds, 0 tens and 8 ones, written in words, and a library total ten above 386 and ten below 406. Check the representation and both answers.
Solve both problems independently. Use a chart or number line and write one complete answer sentence per problem.
Closure · 5 min
Ask pupils to check the library answer against both clues.
Show that 396 is ten above 386 and ten below 406.

lessons.title: Add Ones, Tens and Hundreds
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 p. 46 · Activity Book p. 31
lessons.objective: Find at least three of four sums by adding ones, tens or hundreds, and label one jump correctly on a number line.
lessons.materials: Open number lines, numeral cards and base-ten blocks.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils found three or more totals and labelled one correct jump. Revisit the value of a jump with pupils who moved by the wrong amount.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show 231 and offer a unit cube, a ten rod and a hundred flat. Ask how much each would add.
Match each block to a jump of 1, 10 or 100.
Main activity · 30 min
Model how 231 changes when 5, 40 or 200 is added separately. Show how a long jump can represent several equal small jumps.
Represent each addend with blocks, then draw a jump and write the new total. Swap start cards with a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 304 + 5, 304 + 60, 304 + 200 and 421 + 30. Check the sums and the direction and size of one labelled jump.
Independently find the four totals and draw a labelled jump for one. Use Activity Book p. 31 for further practice if available.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which digit changes when 40 is added to 212.
Name the tens digit and give 252 as the total.

lessons.title: Add Two Numbers Without Regrouping
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 47–48 · Activity Book pp. 32–34
lessons.objective: Align digits by place value and find at least three of four sums without regrouping.
lessons.materials: Hundreds-tens-ones mats, base-ten blocks, mini-whiteboards and pencils.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils aligned and solved at least three items correctly. Give pupils who misaligned digits a labelled place-value mat for the next task.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Place 54 below 312 with 5 in the hundreds column. Ask pupils to move the digits to their correct places.
Put 5 under the tens and 4 under the ones. Explain why.
Main activity · 30 min
Model 312 + 54 on the mat. Transfer the model to vertical form, then show a second example with a zero in the tens place.
Build and add two numbers on the mat. Record each sum in columns and check the column headings before adding.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 241 + 36, 405 + 73, 133 + 246 and 510 + 208. Check both alignment and the sum for each item.
Independently write and solve all four in columns. Use Activity Book pp. 32–34 for follow-up if available.
Closure · 5 min
Ask where to write the 7 when 7 is added to 640.
Place 7 in the ones column and give the total.

lessons.title: Add Two Numbers With Regrouping
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 51–55 · Activity Book pp. 35–37
lessons.objective: Solve at least three of four additions that require regrouping, and explain one exchange using place-value language.
lessons.materials: Base-ten blocks, a place-value mat and squared paper.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils solved at least three and explained one exchange. Revisit the specific column where each pupil lost a regrouped unit.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Put eight and five unit cubes in the ones column. Ask pupils to show the same quantity using fewer blocks.
Exchange ten cubes for one ten rod and identify the three remaining ones.
Main activity · 30 min
Model 148 + 75 with blocks. Record each exchange above the receiving column in vertical form. Then compare with a tens-to-hundreds example.
Build and solve examples with a partner. Point to each exchange on the mat and show where it appears in the written calculation.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 246 + 17, 365 + 72, 287 + 156 and 506 + 194. Check the totals and ask pupils to explain one exchange.
Independently solve all four sums and explain one exchange with blocks, a drawing or a sentence. Use Activity Book pp. 35–37 if available.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what happens if a ten rod is formed but left in the ones column.
Move the rod to tens and explain why the total would otherwise be wrong.

lessons.title: Add Two Numbers Near 1,000
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 56–57 · Activity Book p. 38 (section reference printed on p. 56)
lessons.objective: Find three exact totals within 1,000, including one equal to 1,000, and identify which of the other two totals is closer to 1,000.
lessons.materials: Place-value mats with a thousands column, base-ten blocks and numeral cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils found all three totals and identified the nearer of the two totals below 1,000. Practise the hundreds-to-thousands exchange where needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show nine hundred flats and ask what one more flat makes.
Exchange ten hundreds for one thousand and name the result.
Main activity · 30 min
Model 476 + 524 and show how the exchanges produce one thousand. Offer two sums just below 1,000 and compare the completed totals.
Add the pairs on the mat, record the totals and say which is closer to 1,000.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 420 + 569, 486 + 512 and 735 + 265. Check the three sums and ask which of the two totals below 1,000 is closer to it.
Independently calculate all three sums. Show the last exchange that makes 1,000 and compare the other totals by their distance from 1,000.
Closure · 5 min
Ask where the new 1 belongs when ten hundreds are formed.
Point to thousands and explain why each remaining column shows zero.

lessons.title: Add Three Numbers Within 1,000
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 58–61 · Activity Book pp. 39–41
lessons.objective: Solve at least three of four three-addend sums and explain one useful choice of which two numbers to add first.
lessons.materials: Numeral cards, place-value mats and squared paper.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils found at least three totals and explained one grouping. Give a two-step subtotal prompt to pupils who omitted an addend.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show 145, 55 and 230. Ask which pair makes an easy subtotal.
Choose 145 and 55, then explain how a subtotal of 200 helps.
Main activity · 30 min
Model finding the same total by adding in stages and by aligning all three addends in columns. Include a case where two exchanges occur.
Solve a set of sums with a partner. Compare the two methods and circle a pair that makes a multiple of ten or a hundred.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 123 + 45 + 211, 186 + 34 + 279, 250 + 175 + 325 and 306 + 284 + 410. Check the totals and one grouping explanation.
Independently solve all four sums. Annotate one calculation to show why a chosen pair is useful. Use Activity Book pp. 39–41 if available.
Closure · 5 min
Ask whether changing the order changes the total.
Use one of the sums to explain why the total stays the same.

lessons.title: Subtract Without Regrouping
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 62–65 · Activity Book pp. 42–43
lessons.objective: Find at least three of four differences without regrouping and represent one as backward jumps on a number line.
lessons.materials: Open number lines, base-ten blocks and place-value mats.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils found at least three differences and showed the jumps correctly. Revisit alignment with a labelled mat.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Put down 346 with blocks and remove two ten rods. Ask which place changes.
Name the tens place and say the number left.
Main activity · 30 min
Model 568 − 34 using jumps of 30 and 4, then record the same difference in columns.
Solve pairs of examples with a partner. Match each jump to the place being subtracted.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 684 − 23, 507 − 4, 796 − 352 and 950 − 120. Check the differences and one accurate number line.
Independently find all four differences and draw a labelled number line for one.
Closure · 5 min
Ask where to write the 6 in 769 − 6.
Point to the ones column and give the difference.

lessons.title: Subtract With Regrouping
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 66–72 · Activity Book pp. 44–48
lessons.objective: Find at least three of four differences involving regrouping and explain one exchange across place-value columns.
lessons.materials: Base-ten blocks, place-value mats and squared paper.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils met both checks. Practise regrouping through a zero with pupils who skipped the intermediate column.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show four tens and two ones. Ask how to remove seven ones.
Exchange one ten for ten ones and show the available ones.
Main activity · 30 min
Model 432 − 157 using two exchanges. For 503 − 76, show how to regroup through the zero tens before writing the column calculation.
Build the starting amount, show each exchange and match it to the written changes.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 642 − 25, 851 − 380, 602 − 147 and 500 − 36. Check three or more correct differences and one accurate explanation.
Independently solve all four and explain one exchange using a drawing or words.
Closure · 5 min
Show an exchange where the original column count was left unchanged. Ask for a correction.
Correct the count and explain how the exchange preserves the amount.

lessons.title: Subtract Successively
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 73–75 · Activity Book pp. 49–51
lessons.objective: Find at least three of four differences after two successive subtractions, showing both steps for each correct answer.
lessons.materials: Situation cards, open number lines and squared paper.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils showed both correct steps on at least three items. Provide two labelled spaces for pupils who omitted a step.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Start with 150 tokens on a card. Say that 20 and then 30 are used. Ask for the amount after the first change.
Give 130 and explain which amount should be used for the next step.
Main activity · 30 min
Model 485 − 126 − 94. Write the first difference and use it as the starting value for the second subtraction.
Solve a partner's two-step card and explain which value is the intermediate difference.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 650 − 120 − 55, 724 − 215 − 98, 903 − 175 − 208 and 410 − 109 − 87. Check each intermediate and final difference.
Independently show both steps for all four expressions.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why starting again at the original number gives the wrong final amount.
Point to the intermediate difference and explain the two changes.

lessons.title: Build Equal Groups and Arrays
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 81–83 · Activity Book pp. 56–58
lessons.objective: Represent at least three of four equal-group situations with matching repeated addition, multiplication and totals.
lessons.materials: Counters, paper plates and square grid cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils matched all representations for at least three cards. Use plates to clarify the roles of group count and group size.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Put four counters on each of three plates. Ask which number tells how many plates and which tells how many per plate.
Count the plates and describe the equal groups.
Main activity · 30 min
Model three groups of four as 4 + 4 + 4 and 3 × 4. Rearrange the counters into an array and turn it to compare 3 × 4 and 4 × 3.
Build equal groups, record matching sentences and explain how turning an array keeps the same total.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give cards for 2 groups of 6, 4 groups of 3, 5 groups of 4 and 3 groups of 7. Check the drawing, both sentences and total.
Independently draw and label each group model, then write repeated addition and multiplication for each.
Closure · 5 min
Show groups with different sizes and ask what must change before one multiplication fact can represent them.
Make the groups equal and name the two factors.

lessons.title: Build Facts for 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 84–86 · Activity Book pp. 59–63
lessons.objective: Find at least five of six multiplication facts from the 2 to 6 times tables, and explain one using a known fact.
lessons.materials: Grid cards, counters and blank fact cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils found at least five products and explained one strategy. Rebuild the fact family that caused errors.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show six pairs of counters. Ask how counting in twos finds the total.
Count in twos and record 6 × 2.
Main activity · 30 min
Join two two-column arrays to build a four-column array. Repeat with two three-column arrays for six. Practise facts for five with equal rows.
Build arrays for the 2 to 6 times tables. Use a known product to find a related product in the four or six times table.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 7 × 2, 5 × 3, 6 × 4, 8 × 5, 4 × 6 and 6 × 6. Check five or more products and one valid link between facts.
Independently find each product and show how one known fact helped.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for a quicker way to find 7 × 6 using 7 × 3.
Double 21 and explain why this gives 42.

lessons.title: Build Facts for 7, 8 and 9
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 87–90 · Activity Book pp. 64–67
lessons.objective: Find at least five of six facts from the 7, 8 and 9 times tables, and show one product by splitting an array or using a neighbouring fact.
lessons.materials: Grid paper, counters and highlighters.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils found at least five products and justified one. Revisit the group-size increment with pupils who added only one.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show 5 × 8 as two 5 × 4 rectangles. Ask why the products add.
Count both rectangles and name the full product.
Main activity · 30 min
Model 6 × 7 as 6 × 5 plus 6 × 2. Show how an extra row of nine turns 4 × 9 into 5 × 9.
Split or extend arrays and explain the link to the fact being solved.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 2 × 7, 5 × 7, 3 × 8, 8 × 8, 6 × 9 and 7 × 9. Check the six products and one model with matching calculations.
Independently calculate each product and annotate one array or neighbouring fact.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what happens to the product when one more group of seven is added.
Say it increases by seven and show the extra row.

lessons.title: Multiply by 0, 1 and 10
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 91–93 · Activity Book pp. 68–70
lessons.objective: Find at least five of six products by 0, 1 or 10, with at least one correct product for each factor, and explain a product by ten.
lessons.materials: Empty cups, counters, ten rods and place-value mats.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils met the product and explanation checks. Rebuild the factor cases pupils confused.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show six empty cups and six cups with one counter each. Ask what the two totals are.
Count zero and six, then link each total to its groups.
Main activity · 30 min
Contrast six groups of zero, one and ten. Build 6 × 10 with six ten rods and show why the total is 60.
Build and record matching facts for the three cases, then explain how each factor affects the total.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 7 × 0, 0 × 4, 9 × 1, 1 × 3, 4 × 10 and 8 × 10. Check all three cases and one explanation in tens.
Independently solve all six and show one product by ten using rods or a drawing.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why 5 × 10 is 50.
Explain that five groups of ten make five tens.

lessons.title: Share and Group Equally
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 95–98 · Activity Book pp. 71–74
lessons.objective: Model and solve at least three of four exact division situations, identifying whether the result means the number of groups or the amount per group.
lessons.materials: Counters, paper cups, group mats and number lines.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils modelled and labelled at least three solutions correctly. Repeat both interpretations side by side for pupils who confused them.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show 12 counters and three cups. Ask how to share them equally.
Deal the counters into cups and count how many each cup has.
Main activity · 30 min
Contrast sharing 12 among three cups with making groups of three from 12. Show backward jumps of three for the grouping model.
Build both models, record 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and explain what 4 means in each.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give four tasks: share 18 among 3, group 20 in fives, share 24 among 4 and group 28 in sevens. Check the drawings, equations and what each quotient means.
Independently draw each model, write the equation and label the quotient with its meaning.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how a pupil can tell whether a question gives the number of groups or the group size.
Identify the given quantity in one of the examples.

lessons.title: Use Multiplication to Divide
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 99–103 · Activity Book pp. 75–79
lessons.objective: Solve at least five of six exact division facts and write a related multiplication fact to check one answer.
lessons.materials: Fact-family cards, array grids and mini-whiteboards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils met both checks. Use an array to reconnect a fact that pupils recalled incorrectly.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a 4-by-6 array and cover the row count. Ask how the total and column count help recover it.
Count or use a known fact to find the missing dimension.
Main activity · 30 min
Use 4 × 6 = 24 to build two division facts. Model finding a missing factor with 42 ÷ 7.
Build fact families with a partner and use the related multiplication fact to check each quotient.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 21 ÷ 3, 36 ÷ 4, 40 ÷ 5, 42 ÷ 6, 56 ÷ 8 and 63 ÷ 9. Check at least five correct quotients and one multiplication check.
Independently solve all six and write a matching product for one.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what multiplication fact checks 54 ÷ 6 = 9.
Give 6 × 9 = 54 and point to 9 as the factor that was missing.

lessons.title: Divide by One and Use Zero as the Dividend
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 104–106 · Activity Book p. 80 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Find at least four of five quotients involving a divisor of one, a zero dividend or equal positive numbers, and explain one case.
lessons.materials: Counters, cups and fact cards. All examples have a non-zero divisor.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils gave at least four correct quotients and one explanation. Use empty cups to revisit the zero-dividend case.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Place eight counters in one cup. Ask how many the one cup receives.
Give eight and connect it to 8 ÷ 1.
Main activity · 30 min
Compare sharing a set with one recipient, sharing zero among several recipients and placing one counter into each of as many cups as counters.
Act out each case, write the related fact and explain what stays the same.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 6 ÷ 1, 9 ÷ 1, 0 ÷ 5, 0 ÷ 8 and 7 ÷ 7. Check the quotients and one explanation using counters or a matching multiplication fact.
Independently solve the five facts and explain one.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what each of three cups receives when there are no counters to share.
Give zero and connect the answer to 0 ÷ 3.

lessons.title: Divide With a Remainder
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 109–113
lessons.objective: Find the quotient and remainder in at least three of four one-digit-divisor problems and show why one remainder is smaller than the divisor.
lessons.materials: Counters, group mats and basic-fact cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils calculated at least three quotient-remainder pairs and explained one check. Rebuild a worked example for pupils who stopped before forming all full groups.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Ask pupils to group 13 counters in fours. Discuss what happens to the loose counter.
Make three full groups and identify the one left over.
Main activity · 30 min
Use 29 ÷ 6 to find the largest multiple of six below 29. Show how the remainder is what is left after forming the full groups.
Build several groups with counters, then record quotient and remainder and check both using multiplication and addition.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 17 ÷ 3, 23 ÷ 4, 31 ÷ 6 and 43 ÷ 8. Check three or more correct pairs and one explanation about the size of the remainder.
Independently solve each and show why the remainder in one answer cannot make another full group.
Closure · 5 min
Ask whether 3 remainder 6 can be a finished answer when dividing by five.
Explain that six can make another full group of five.

lessons.title: Divide Two-Digit Numbers by Ten
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 105–107 and 114–115 · Activity Book pp. 81–82 (remainder-section reference)
lessons.objective: Find at least three of four quotients and remainders, including one exact division and one with a non-zero remainder, and explain one using tens and ones.
lessons.materials: Ten rods, unit cubes, bundle mats and mini-whiteboards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils met the quotient and remainder checks. Revisit the distinction between packs and objects with loose-cube examples.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show 40 counters as four bundles of ten. Ask how many full packs of ten can be made.
Name the four packs and say that none are left.
Main activity · 30 min
Contrast 60 ÷ 10 with 64 ÷ 10. Explain that a full ten gives one pack and the loose ones are the remainder.
Model each case using rods and cubes and record the quotient and remainder.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 30 ÷ 10, 54 ÷ 10, 80 ÷ 10 and 97 ÷ 10. Check both types of result and one place-value explanation.
Independently solve all four and draw the full tens and loose ones for one.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why the remainder is zero for 80 ÷ 10.
Explain that all 80 objects fit into eight full packs of ten.

lessons.title: Create Addition and Subtraction Stories
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 76–77 · Activity Book pp. 52–53
lessons.objective: Create two realistic stories, one for addition and one for subtraction, using both numbers in the given roles and ending with a suitable question.
lessons.materials: Number-sentence cards, classroom item pictures and story planning cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils created two stories that met all checks. Practise stating the starting amount and change with pupils who reversed them.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two baskets of the same item. Ask for a question that requires finding the combined total.
Make a question asking how many items there are altogether.
Main activity · 30 min
Model a join story and a take-away story. Highlight which quantities are given and which the question asks for.
Draft one story with a partner, then swap stories and check that each matches the number sentence.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 236 + 147 and 560 − 128. Check that both numbers have correct roles, the unit is consistent and the question asks for the intended unknown.
Independently write or dictate two stories and include a matching question for each.
Closure · 5 min
Read a story that uses a subtraction question with an addition card. Ask for a correction.
Revise the question or the action so the story matches the card.

lessons.title: Solve Addition and Subtraction Stories
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 78–80 · Activity Book pp. 54–55
lessons.objective: Choose the correct operation and solve two everyday problems using a representation and a sentence with the correct unit.
lessons.materials: Bar-model strips, base-ten blocks and problem cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils solved both problems with valid representations and units. Use aligned bars to reteach comparison where needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Describe two groups bringing craft paper. Ask which quantities are the parts and what is unknown.
Identify the two parts and the missing whole.
Main activity · 30 min
Model a part-part-whole diagram and a comparison diagram. Ask pupils to choose the operation from what is unknown.
Draw a bar for each practice problem, write the number sentence and check if the result is reasonable.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask for the total when classes bring 245 and 178 cards. Ask how many more cards there are in a box of 507 than in a box of 368. Check both equations, representations and answer sentences.
Independently solve both problems and label each answer in cards.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how to check a difference of 139 between 507 and 368.
Add 139 to 368 to check the larger total.

lessons.title: Create Multiplication and Division Stories
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 116–117 · Activity Book pp. 83–84
lessons.objective: Create one equal-groups multiplication story and one grouping division story that correctly interprets a remainder.
lessons.materials: Blank story cards, counters and cups.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils created two consistent stories and interpreted the remainder correctly. Give a concrete grouping prompt where the story roles were unclear.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show four trays with six counters each. Ask for a question that uses the groups.
Ask how many counters there are altogether.
Main activity · 30 min
Model writing a question for equal groups. Then model a grouping story and show how the leftover amount fits the context.
Match each story to an arrangement of counters. Swap a draft with a partner to check that the groups and leftover are realistic.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give 5 × 4 = 20 and 29 ÷ 6 = 4 remainder 5. Check that both stories assign quantities correctly and ask about the intended unknown.
Independently write or dictate one story for each equation. Include the question about full groups and leftover items in the division story.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why the five leftover items cannot fill another group of six.
Explain the remainder in terms of the story.

lessons.title: Solve Multiplication and Division Stories
lessons.references: Textbook Part 1 pp. 118–121 · Activity Book pp. 85–86 (section reference printed on p. 120)
lessons.objective: Select the operation and solve two equal-group problems, interpreting the quotient and remainder in the division problem.
lessons.materials: Situation cards, counters, square grids and number-sentence slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils chose both operations and interpreted both answers correctly. Use concrete groups for pupils who confused full packs with the number per pack.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show several packs holding the same number of items and a separate pile to be packed. Ask what is already known in each situation.
Identify group size and group count in the first case, and the total and pack size in the second.
Main activity · 30 min
Model an array for an equal-group total and a grouping diagram for packing a fixed total. Use a related fact to check each calculation.
Choose a model, solve one of each type with a partner and explain what the answer counts.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
